summary: A brick keepers' house on a Delaware Bay caisson, lit in 1910 at the elbow of Cross Ledge; struck by a freighter in 1953 and replaced by a skeleton tower.

lens.note: Barbier, Benard and Turenne, four panels; original 1910 lens

structures.type: octagonal two-story brick keepers' house with iron watchroom and lantern
red steel skeleton tower on the old caisson
structures.note: Dates conflict: 1953 (USLHS), 1954 (Friends web page), 1955 (Friends newsletter). Height 61 ft base to center of lantern (USLHS).

access.note: Owned by the Coast Guard. Tower closed. Best seen from the water. USLHS lists it as not open to the public.

events.note: Lighthouse Board recommends a gas-lighted beacon on an iron caisson at the Elbow (estimated cost not over $60,000) for the new harbor of refuge.
Congress appropriates $75,000 for a lighthouse and fog signal.
September storm sweeps away the working platform; at least one workman drowned; a scow with an inspector adrift for two days.
Congress grants $21,500 more, May 27, 1908, to complete the superstructure.
Official light first exhibited February 1, 1910, by keepers transferred from Cross Ledge.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens, Barbier, Benard and Turenne.
Keeper Julian Bacon's motorboat stalls about four miles out in July 1916; he drifts for three days and swims ashore (as quoted by LighthouseFriends from the New Castle News).
Julian Bacon listed among light stations awarded efficiency flags (Bulletin index, p. 22).
Severe storm along the Middle and North Atlantic coasts, early February 1920; slight damage at Elbow of Cross Ledge (Bulletin).
Station electrified with duplicate 800-watt lighting plants.
Tyfon air horn replaces the fog bell.
Coast Guard automates the light; the four-man crew is removed; control from Miah Maull Shoal.
Steel Apprentice strikes the light in fog on October 20, 1953; the upper two-thirds topples into the bay.
Brick house knocked into the bay; only the caisson base remains.
Red steel skeleton tower erected on the old foundation (1953 per USLHS; 1954 per Friends web page; 1955 per Friends newsletter).
Coast Guard burns what was left of the wreck down to its granite base (Friends newsletter; not confirmed elsewhere).

corrections.why: The Friends' web page says the skeleton tower 'still remains in operation today as an aid to navigation', and the Friends' 2022 newsletter says it is 'still in service today'. The USLHS record says 'Active Aid to Navigation?: No', which predates or disagrees with them. The Coast Guard light list should decide.

corrections.proposed: brick house destroyed 1953; caisson, built 1910, standing
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends and the Friends' web page say the 1953 collision knocked the brick house into the bay, and only the caisson base remained.

notes_for_editor: 1) Printed page 86 of the 1900 Light-House Board report: the OCR page header '86 REPORT OF THE LIGHT-HOUSE BOARD. 1900.' sits about 2,000 characters before the Elbow entry with no page break between; scan page 102 is confirmed by corpus.py. A page image check is still advisable before printing. 2) The Bulletin 1918 efficiency-flag table (PDF p. 22) was matched by column position (the OCR table is not reliable), so the story relies on the clean index entry for Bacon. 3) The 1920 storm text is interleaved in the OCR; the story now describes the early-February storm and the Elbow's slight damage without dating the Elbow entry to 4 February (the 4 February entry is Thimble Shoal and others). 4) Tower dates conflict: 1953 (USLHS 'Year Tower Established'), 1954 (Friends web page; Wikipedia lead infobox gives first lit 1954), 1955 (Friends newsletter 'erected and relit in 1955'). Unresolved. 5) Status conflict: USLHS 'Active Aid to Navigation?: No' vs Friends sources (in service, solarized 1998). The Coast Guard light list record (LLNR 2-1600) was not read. 6) The 1962 burning of the wreck and the 1951 storm are told in the newsletter's 'That Was Then' passage, which opens with the original Cross Ledge light; the text places them after the Elbow's history, so check which structure is meant. 7) The 1907 storm, the 1916 drift and the 1910 visitors are second-hand (LighthouseFriends quoting the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin, New Castle News and Bridgeton Evening News). Chronicling America searches for 1910 and 1953 returned nothing usable. 8) The USCG Historian's archived page returned no body text and is not cited. 9) Record position: USLHS (39 deg 10.9 min N, 75 deg 16.1 min W), LighthouseFriends (39.182226, -75.268443) and the Wikipedia lead infobox agree with the record (39.182235, -75.268448) within about 10 m. The record's 'more than 500 m apart' conflict is not explained by any source read. 10) Roster: Harry J. Wilson's span 1911.09.31-1911.11.06 prints an impossible date; recorded as 1911. 11) Wikipedia is a lead only and is not cited.
